Heteropolar (heterolytic) fission breaks a covalent bond unevenly.
The shared pair leaves with the more electronegative atom.
A : B ⇒ A⁺ + B⁻ — one fragment keeps both electrons, the other keeps none.
So the fragments carry charge: one cation and one anion.
Free radicals (1) come from homolytic fission, where the pair splits one each.
∴ heteropolar reactions go through both anions and cations.

Kjeldahl's method works only when the nitrogen is converted to ammonium sulphate by hot conc. H₂SO₄.
That needs the N to be in an easily hydrolysed form, as in amines and amides.
In pyridine the nitrogen sits inside an aromatic ring, held by the delocalised π system.
It resists digestion, so it is never converted to (NH₄)₂SO₄ and never released as NH₃.
Statement I (it cannot be estimated) is therefore true.
Statement II (it does change to ammonium sulphate) contradicts that, so it is false.
∴ Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

Chain isomers differ in how the carbon skeleton is branched, not in any functional group.
For C₅H₁₂ build every distinct skeleton of 5 carbons:
1. straight chain — n-pentane, C-C-C-C-C
2. one methyl branch on a 4-carbon chain — 2-methylbutane (isopentane)
3. two methyl branches on a 3-carbon chain — 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane)
3-methylbutane is not new; numbering from the other end makes it 2-methylbutane.
∴ 3 chain isomers.

The formula fits the alkane series CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Check: 2n + 2 = 2(20) + 2 = 42 ✓, so this is the straight-chain alkane with n = 20.
Alkane names follow the Greek numeral for n: dec- = 10, dodec- = 12, eicos- = 20.
Decane is C₁₀H₂₂ and dodecane is C₁₂H₂₆, both too small.
"Hicosane" is not a valid name.
∴ C₂₀H₄₂ is eicosane.

In chlorobenzene the lone pair on Cl is delocalised into the ring.
That gives the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character, so it is shorter and stronger,
and the carbon is sp² — smaller orbital, shorter bond.
In methyl chloride the carbon is sp³ and no resonance is possible; the bond is a pure single bond.
Comparing CH₃Cl against C₆H₅Cl, then, the bond in CH₃Cl is the longer one and the weaker one.
∴ longer and weaker.

Work through each starting material.
Benzene: direct chlorination, Cl₂ with anhydrous AlCl₃ or FeCl₃ ⇒ chlorobenzene, easy.
Aniline: diazotise with NaNO₂/HCl at 273–278 K, then Sandmeyer with CuCl ⇒ chlorobenzene, easy.
Benzene diazonium chloride: that is the same Sandmeyer step, one stage shorter ⇒ easy.
Phenol: the C–O bond has partial double-bond character from resonance with the ring,
so –OH is not replaced by Cl under ordinary conditions.
∴ chlorobenzene cannot easily be prepared from phenol.
